name: Lanolin
lead: Lanolin is a yellow, waxy substance secreted by the sebaceous glands of wool-bearing animals, mainly sheep, and recovered from wool washing; it is often called wool fat or wool wax although it is mainly sterol and wax esters rather than a true fat.[1][2] Purified lanolin is a widely used emollient in skin care, lip balms, baby products and nipple creams, and it resembles lipids of human skin.[1][2]

Lanolin is also a relatively common contact allergen, and Wikipedia describes the question of how sensitizing it really is as historically contested.[1] Registered trials have compared lanolin with other topicals for sore nipples in breastfeeding women; Wikipedia states that evidence for a soothing effect is limited.[1][3][4]
infobox: Moisturizers, lip balm, nipple care, industrial coatings
Recognized contact allergen; purified low-allergen grades exist

paras: Crude lanolin makes up roughly 5 to 25 percent of the weight of freshly shorn wool; wool is washed in hot water and detergent and the grease is separated by centrifuge, then refined to a waxy solid.[1] High-purity grades are about 97 percent long-chain esters, with an estimated several thousand ester types, and derivatives are made by hydrolysis, esterification and related processes.[1] Grokipedia reports that it can absorb up to 200 percent of its weight in water and forms water-in-oil emulsions.[2]

In skin care lanolin acts as a long-acting emollient; Wikipedia notes studies suggesting it outperforms petrolatum for very dry hands and superficial wound healing, and it is used in lip balms such as Carmex, though some people find it irritating to the lips.[1] It is also used on sore nipples during breastfeeding, and in industrial products such as boat coatings, leather care and lubricants.[1]

Lanolin allergy is often mistaken for wool allergy, and patch testing is used to confirm it.[1] A 1950s study found about 1 percent of dermatology patients allergic, but Wikipedia reports that the lack of a healthy comparison group later was estimated to exaggerate its sensitizing potential greatly; a 1976 European labelling requirement was overturned in the early 1980s.[1] Pharmacopoeia limits on pesticide residues were added in the US in 1992 and Europe in 2000, and ultra-purified grades are marketed as low-allergen.[1] Standardized patch-test series such as those of the North American Contact Dermatitis Group include lanolin-related allergens among those monitored.[5]

Registered trials of lanolin focus on breastfeeding care: one compares lanolin with breast milk for sore and damaged nipples (206 participants), another evaluates lanolin for nipple pain (186 participants), another compares two treatments for healing nipple wounds, and another compares highly purified anhydrous lanolin with coconut oil for preventing subacute lactation mastitis.[3][4][6][7] Results were not available for review. No trials of lanolin for cosmetic or appearance purposes were found.

timeline.event: European Cosmetics Directive requires labelling of lanolin-containing cosmetics; later overturned in the early 1980s.[1]
US Pharmacopoeia adds pesticide limits and a Modified Lanolin standard.[1]
European Pharmacopoeia adds pesticide residue limits.[1]

card.summary: A wool-derived emollient wax in lip balms and moisturizers, with allergy history and trials aimed mainly at sore nipples.
card.aka: Wool wax, wool fat, wool grease
card.note: A recognized contact allergen for some people; purified grades are sold as low-allergen.

quick.overview:
Lanolin is a waxy substance from sheep wool that is refined into an emollient for moisturizers, lip balms, baby care and nipple creams.

It is described as long-lasting at holding moisture, but registered trials focus on breastfeeding nipple care and none were found for cosmetic purposes.
quick.mechanism: Its sterol and wax esters resemble skin lipids; it forms an occlusive layer and can take up water, which is why it is described as an emollient.
quick.risks: It is a relatively common contact allergen, though Wikipedia says its sensitizing potential was historically overstated. Purified, low-pesticide grades are standardized in the US and European pharmacopoeias.
